content.text: Students connect Chapter 20 to civil rights activism by comparing scientific teamwork with student-led social protest.
Scientific discovery and social change both grow through organized effort, evidence, and people pushing against limits.

content.text: Directions:
First, look closely at the image. Then turn to your partner and share one detail you notice and one idea you have about how this scene connects to the ideas you have been exploring in this unit.
What do you notice in this visual, and how might it connect to the Ideas we have been exploring in Hidden Figures?
Using Context Clues
Target Word:
monitor
In Chapter 20, the text explains, "Together these three computers would be able to monitor and analyze all aspects of the space flights, from launch to splashdown."
Identify Context Clues
Directions:
With a partner, discuss: What is happening in the sentence? Which words or phrases help explain the meaning of monitor? Then, underline the clues in the displayed text.
Infer a Meaning
Based on the clues, what does the word most likely mean?
Test the Meaning in Context
If we replace the word with our meaning, does the sentence still make sense?
Verify Meaning
Check your definition using a dictionary or other reference material. Does the definition match what we figured out?
Quick Application
Did the context give us enough information to figure this word out? How might we confirm the meaning if we aren’t sure?
Check for Understanding
List the word monitor in your
Personal Dictionary
. After each word, write (1) the definition of the word and (2) the word in a sentence.
Part A: Seeing Collaboration Across Sources

We are going to compare how different types of sources help us understand the same idea. Each source adds something different. Your job is to figure out what each one contributes and how they work together to convey an idea about the power of collaboration.
Directions:
Using the 3-column chart to compare multiple sources. Label each column as indicated:
Column 1: Greensboro Lunch Counter (Visual)
Column 2: Sit-Ins Text (Informational)
Column 3: Chapter 20 (Narrative/Informational)
In each column, write:
One important detail from that source (what it shows or explains)
What this helps you understand about collaboration or working together for shared purpose
Be sure to use information directly from each source.
Pulse Check
Which statement best integrates the Greensboro lunch counter and Chapter 20?
A. The Greensboro lunch counter is about restaurants, while Chapter 20 is only about machines, so the sources do not really connect.
B. Both sources show people acting alone to solve private problems.
C. Both the sit-in movement and the tracking network depended on coordinated groups working toward greater access—civil rights in one case and space discovery in the other.
D. Chapter 20 is more useful than the Greensboro lunch counter because written texts always give more information than images.

Directions:

Use the RACE organizer to answer the text-dependent question in four to five sentences. Include at least one detail from the Sit-Ins visual or text and at least one detail from Chapter 20. Use one comparative transition from today’s lesson, such as

or

In Chapter 20, how do the student sit-ins and the development of global tracking systems both show people working together overcome limitations and boundaries?
Reflection
Reflect on your reading and writing abilities using the Reflection routine.
How confident are you in your ability to combine a visual and a written source into one explanation?

Directions:

For your Quick Write, explain how today’s sit-ins sources changed or deepened your understanding of Chapter 20. Use two specific details—one from the civil rights source set and one from Chapter 20—and explain what those details show together. This is the same kind of source integration you will need for the Hidden Innovators performance task.

First, look closely at the image. Then turn to your partner and share one detail you notice and one idea you have about how this scene connects to the ideas you have been exploring in this unit.
Ask:
What do you notice in this visual, and how might it connect to the Ideas we have been exploring in
Hidden Figures
I notice that the students are sitting close together and staying in place even though the setting looks tense. This connects to our unit because, like the women in
Hidden Figures
, they seem to be working together to challenge a boundary that is unjust.
Teacher Tip
Give brief context before discussion: a
sit-in

was a nonviolent protest in which students sat at segregated lunch counters and refused to leave. For sixth graders, anchor the discussion in fairness, courage, and teamwork rather than assuming detailed prior knowledge of the civil rights timeline.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
Now we will learn some key vocabulary that will help us integrate sources as we explain our ideas.
Students will look at images and draw conclusions about how they connect to the ideas explored in this unit.
Using Context Clues
Target Word: monitor
Display the Key Sentences
In Chapter 20, the text explains, "Together these three computers would be able to
monitor
and analyze all aspects of the space flights, from launch to splashdown."
Say:

This sentence includes a word we may not fully understand yet. Instead of looking them up right away, we’re going to use context clues—the words around them—to figure out what they most likely mean. Our focus word today is
monitor
Identify Context Clues
Say these Directions: With a partner, discuss: What is happening in the sentence? Which words or phrases help explain the meaning of
monitor
? Then, underline the clues in the displayed text.
“and analyze all aspects”
Infer a Meaning
Ask:
Based on the clues, what does the word most likely mean?
Monitor means to watch or track something carefully over time.
Test the Meaning in Context
Ask:
If we replace the word with our meaning, does the sentence still make sense?
Yes, when I replace monitor with “watch carefully,” the sentence still makes sense.
Verify Meaning
Say:
Check your definition using a dictionary or other reference material. Does the definition match what we figured out? Revise as needed.
Quick Application
Ask:
Did the context give us enough information to figure this word out? How might we confirm the meaning if we aren’t sure?
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
Now that we have precise language for scientific tracking, we are ready to compare what each source contributes.
Check for Understanding
List the word
monitor
in your Personal Dictionary. After each word, write (1) the definition of the word and (2) the word in a sentence.
Support students in determining word meaning from context and then using precise academic nouns and verbs to prepare for source integration.
Language Focus:
Context clue language
Precise academic nouns
Definition frames
If students define a word too broadly, press for the action in the sentence that narrows the meaning.
Encourage students to restate the meaning in their own words after verifying it so they do not simply copy a dictionary entry.
“You said ‘monitor means keep checking’—we can say: ‘To monitor means to watch and track something carefully over time.’”
“The clue ___ helped me infer that ___ means ___.”
“In this sentence, the word ___ probably means ___ because ___.”
“After checking the reference tool, I would revise my definition to ___.”
Invite students to notice if monitor has a cognate or familiar school/community use in a language they know and then connect that to the sentence context.
If students define monitor as fix or control → Prompt: “Which words in the sentence show watching and tracking instead of changing something directly?”
Students cite the exact clue phrase that shaped their inference.
Students revise vague definitions into precise, sentence-based meanings.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Using Context Clues
Have students underline the clue phrase before writing a definition and use the frame “The words ___ show that ___ means ___.”
Struggling with: Moving from Everyday Language to Academic Language
Let students first say the meaning in their own words and then revise with a partner using one precise noun, such as ‘monitoring.’
Ready for extension

Have students write a contrast sentence using the target word and a transition such as 'while' or 'similarly'. For students who would benefit from an alternative means of expression, allow an oral recording of the definition sentence or the use of speech-to-text in place of handwritten notes.
Explicitly teach students to use context clues and reference tools to define key social and scientific terms needed for synthesis of sources.
Part A: Seeing Collaboration Across Sources (RI.6.7) (15 minutes)

Students work with a partner to integrate information across multiple formats (informational text and visual) to build a more complete understanding of a shared topic. Rather than evaluating sources, students identify what each source contributes and how the sources work together to develop ideas such as collaboration, coordination, and shared purpose.
Have students work in pairs with Chapter 20, one of the Sit-Ins texts from the linked set, and the Greensboro lunch counter images.
Say:

We are going to compare how different types of sources help us understand the same idea. Each source adds something different. Your job is to figure out what each one contributes and how they work together to convey an idea about the power of collaboration.
Say these Directions:
Using the 3-column chart to compare multiple sources. Label each column as indicated:
Column 1: Greensboro Lunch Counter (Visual)
Column 2: Sit-Ins Text (Informational)
Column 3: Chapter 20 (Narrative/Informational)
Say these Directions:
In each column, write:
One important detail from that source (what it shows or explains)
What this helps you understand about collaboration or working together for shared purpose
Be sure to use information directly from each source.
Teach:
Say:

When I integrate sources, I think about what each one does best. The visual helps me see body language and group positioning. The informational text explains how actions were organized. Chapter 20 shows how collaboration can happen across different places within a scientific system. Then I ask: What do I understand better when I put these sources together?
Ask:
What do the Greensboro lunch counter images add that the written Sit-Ins text does not add by itself?
The visual adds body language and group positioning. I can see students sitting shoulder to shoulder and staying calm, which helps me understand the courage and coordination behind the protest.
Ask:
How does the section of Chapter 20 that explains the worldwide tracking network show collaboration in a different context?
Chapter 20 shows collaboration through a scientific system spread across many places. Workers in different tracking stations had to coordinate and monitor the capsule so the mission could succeed.
Sample Response for Chart
Column 1 (Greensboro Lunch Counter): Students sit together at a lunch counter while others stand behind them. This helps me understand organized protest and shared courage.
Column 2 (Sit-Ins Text): Students used sit-ins to challenge segregation. This helps me understand that change depended on planned group action.
Column 3 (Chapter 20): Tracking stations around the world worked together to follow the mission. This helps me understand scientific teamwork across a global network.
Pulse Check (RI.6.7)
Which statement best integrates the Greensboro lunch counter and Chapter 20?
A. The Greensboro lunch counter is about restaurants, while Chapter 20 is only about machines, so the sources do not really connect.
Incorrect: This choice notices a topic difference but misses the deeper connection between organized human action in both sources.
B. Both sources show people acting alone to solve private problems.
Incorrect: This choice reflects the misconception that the sources are centered on individuals rather than coordinated groups.
C. Both the sit-in movement and the tracking network depended on coordinated groups working toward greater access—civil rights in one case and space discovery in the other.
Correct: This choice synthesizes the sources around a shared idea and identifies how each source develops that idea in a different domain.
D. Chapter 20 is more useful than the Greensboro lunch counter because written texts always give more information than images.
Incorrect: This choice evaluates source type instead of integrating what each source contributes.
Support students in integrating information across sources by explaining what each source contributes and how at least two sources work together to develop the idea of collaboration.
Language Focus:
Comparative transitions (both, while, similarly)
Source-integration frames
Precise academic nouns (collaboration, coordination, protest, system)
Before Reading and Note-Taking (preparation step—optional)
Have students orally rehearse:
One sentence using: The visual shows ___.
One sentence using: The text explains ___.
If students describe only what they see → Ask: “What action or shared goal do these details suggest?”
If students summarize one source only → Prompt: “Use both or while to connect this idea to another source.”
If students name two sources but do not connect them → Ask: “What do these sources show about working together?”
“You said ‘the picture has a lot of students’—we can say: ‘The visual emphasizes coordinated protest by showing students acting side by side.’”
“That idea connects to the text because both sources highlight people working together toward a shared goal.”
“The visual shows ___, while the text explains ___.”
“Both sources develop the idea of collaboration by ___.”
“Chapter 20 adds ___, which helps me understand ___.”
Provide a brief turn-and-talk before writing so students can clarify ideas, including use of a shared home language if helpful.
If students list details without integration → Prompt: “Start with ‘Both sources show’ or ‘While the visual shows.’”
If students begin with a comparison but stop → Prompt: “Finish by naming the shared action, goal, or system.”
Students identify what the visual contributes beyond the text.
Students connect at least two sources using a comparative phrase.
Students name a shared idea (e.g., collaboration, coordination) rather than listing details.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Integrating Visual Evidence
Prompt students to complete the frame “The image detail ___ suggests ___ because ___.”
Struggling with: Abstract Comparison
Have students first name the action in each source and then name the shared category: protest, monitoring, coordination, or collaboration.
Ready for extension
Ask students to add a fourth column labeled freedom/discovery and explain which type of freedom each source pushes toward.

Have students compare how physical closeness in the visual differs from long-distance coordination in Chapter 20, while still counting as collaboration. For students who would benefit from an alternative means of expression, allow them to talk through one organizer row aloud with a partner before writing or use speech-to-text for the connection sentence.
Learning in Action B: Writing a Synthesis Response (RI.6.7)
(15 minutes)
RACE Strategy Response
Teach: Building a Synthesis Claim
Say:

A synthesized response weaves together details from multiple sources to develop a single, connected idea; it is not the same as placing two separate source summaries back‑to‑back. I begin by identifying the shared idea that connects the sources; for our work today, that idea is collaboration. Then I select one specific detail from the sit‑ins source set and one from Chapter 20 that strongly support that idea. After that, I explain the common idea the two sources share. I also make sure my transitions actually do meaningful work—
while
helps to highlight differences, and
both

helps to emphasize similarities. Finally, I check that my response fully answers the question: How do these examples show people pushing for new freedoms and discovery? If any part is missing, I revise until the answer is complete and clear.
Display the following writing model if needed for support and guidance. Point out each RACE element if extra support is needed.

Both the student sit-ins and the global tracking system in Chapter 20 show people working together to push past limits. In the sit-in sources, students acted as a group to challenge segregation and demand equal treatment in public spaces. In Chapter 20, workers across multiple tracking stations monitored the mission together so NASA could follow the capsule and keep the project moving. This matters because one group was pushing for more social freedom, while the other was expanding scientific discovery. Together, the sources show that progress often depends on organized people who refuse to accept old boundaries.
Say these Directions:

Use the RACE organizer to answer the text-dependent question in four to five sentences. Include at least one detail from the Sit-Ins visual or text and at least one detail from Chapter 20. Use one comparative transition from today’s lesson, such as
both, similarly, while
, or
in contrast
Ask:
In Chapter 20, how do the student sit-ins and the development of global tracking systems both show people working together overcome limitations and boundaries?

Both examples show that progress happens when groups organize toward a common goal. In the sit-in sources, students worked together through demonstrations to challenge segregation and demand more freedom in everyday life. In Chapter 20, NASA depended on tracking stations around the world to monitor the mission, which shows scientific collaboration across long distances. While one group was pushing for civil rights and the other was supporting space exploration, both were expanding what people believed was possible. This is demonstrated in the text by, “In February 1960, four Black students from North Carolina A&T staged non-violent protests by sitting at a segregated lunch counter and refusing to leave.”
Reflection (RI.6.7)
Reflect on your reading and writing abilities using the
Reflection
routine.
How confident are you in your ability to combine a visual and a written source into one explanation?
Support students in writing a concise synthesis response that connects evidence from different source types to one clear idea.
Language Focus:
Analytical transitions
Source-based explanation
Precise academic nouns
If students write one source at a time without synthesis, ask them to revise the topic sentence first so it names the shared idea.
If students use a transition inaccurately, have them reread the sentence and decide whether they are showing similarity or difference.
“You said ‘both are about change’—we can say: ‘Both sources show coordinated action aimed at expanding freedom or discovery.’”
You said ‘NASA people were helping’—we can say: ‘Chapter 20 highlights a global monitoring system that depended on scientific collaboration.’”
“Both sources show collaboration because ___.”
“The sit-in source emphasizes ___, while Chapter 20 emphasizes ___.”
“This source pairing deepens my understanding by ___.”
Allow students to orally rehearse their full response with a partner before writing, including use of a shared home language to clarify ideas before drafting in English.
If students copy details without explaining significance → Prompt: “Add a sentence beginning with ‘This matters because.’”
If students confuse comparison with contrast → Prompt: “Ask yourself: Am I showing a similarity, a difference, or both? Then choose the transition that matches.”
Students include evidence from at least two sources in one organized response.
Students use a comparative transition accurately and explain the shared idea, not just the separate details.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Organizing a Synthesis Response
Have them use this oral plan before writing: shared idea → sit-in detail → Chapter 20 detail → why it matters.
Struggling with: Transition Choice
Offer a quick decision prompt: Use both or similarly for a shared action; use while or in contrast for a difference.
Ready for extension
Challenge students to add one sentence explaining why these two kinds of collaboration belong together in a chapter about freedom.

Ask students to revise one sentence to make the academic nouns more precise by using words such as demonstration, monitoring, or coordination. For students who would benefit from an alternative means of expression, allow an oral rehearsal recording before drafting or let students use speech-to-text for the written response.
Part A: Seeing Collaboration Across Sources (RI.6.7)
Students will use a 3-Column Chart to integrate ideas from the Greensboro lunch counter images, a Sit-Ins text, and Chapter 20.
Part B: Writing a Synthesis Response (RI.6.7)
Students will answer the text-dependent question using evidence from visual and written sources.
Transition students from drafting to reflection by reminding them that good readers learn not only from sources, but also from the tools they used to connect them.
Quick Write
Say these Directions:
For your
Quick Write

, explain how today’s sit-ins sources changed or deepened your understanding of Chapter 20. Use two specific details—one from the civil rights source set and one from Chapter 20—and explain what those details show together. This is the same kind of source integration you will need for the Hidden Innovators performance task.

The Greensboro lunch counter images deepened my understanding of Chapter 20 because it made collaboration look more personal and brave. In the visual, the students stay seated together at the counter, which shows organized resistance. In Chapter 20, the tracking stations around the world had to monitor the mission together, which shows organized scientific teamwork. Together, these details show that people can work together to challenge unfair barriers and expand discovery at the same time. The text supports this response by stating, “Four Black students sat down at a whites‑only lunch counter . . . and asked to be served.”
Optional Sentence Starter:
Both the sit-ins sources and Chapter 20 show ___, but they do it in different ways.
Students will reflect on how multiple sources can deepen their understanding of collaboration and freedom.
Instruct students to:
Read and annotate Chapter 21 of
Hidden Figures
Read “Glenn Orbits the Earth” and annotate for details about collaboration, evidence, and mission success.

standards.description: Use context (e.g., the overall meaning of a sentence or paragraph; a word’s position or function in a sentence) as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
Verify the preliminary determination of the meaning of a word or phrase (e.g., by checking the inferred meaning in context or in a dictionary).
Integrate information presented in different media or formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively) as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.
Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
By the end of the year, read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 6–8 text complexity band proficiently, with scaffolding as needed at the high end of the range.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Produce clear and coherent writing in which the development, organization, and style are appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.

Use knowledge of morphology (e.g., affixes, roots, and base words), context, reference materials, and visual cues to determine the meaning, including figurative and connotative meanings, of unknown and multiple‐meaning words on a variety of new topics.
Use knowledge of morphology (e.g., affixes, roots, and base words), context, reference materials, and visual cues to determine the meaning of unknown and multiple‐meaning words on familiar topics.

Use knowledge of morphology (e.g., affixes, roots, and base words), context, reference materials, and visual cues to determine the meaning of unknown and multiple‐meaning words on familiar and new topics.

Explain how well writers and speakers use specific language resources to present ideas or support arguments and provide detailed evidence (e.g., identifying the specific language used to present ideas and claims that are well supported and distinguishing them from those that are not), with light support.

Explain how well writers and speakers use language to support ideas and arguments with detailed evidence (e.g., identifying the precise vocabulary used to present evidence, or the phrasing used to signal a shift in meaning), with substantial support.

Explain how well writers and speakers use specific language to present ideas or support arguments and provide detailed evidence (e.g., showing the clarity of the phrasing used to present an argument), with moderate support.

Expand noun phrases in an increasing variety of ways (e.g., adding comparative/superlative and general academic adjectives to noun phrases or more complex clause embedding) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and add details about ideas, people, things, and the like.
Expand noun phrases in simple ways (e.g., adding a sensory adjective to a noun) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and add details about ideas, people, things, and the like.

Expand noun phrases in a variety of ways (e.g., adding comparative/superlative adjectives to noun phrases or simple clause embedding) in order to enrich the meaning of sentences and add details about ideas, people, things, and the like.
